title: Rule20 Permissive Joinder
subject: Civil Procedure
stem: After a roofing company moved to sever, two plaintiffs argued that they could proceed together in one federal negligence action. Daniel alleges that he was hurt in January when bundled shingles slid from a pallet at the company's Virginia supply yard. Martha alleges that she was injured in July when a ladder fell from a different crew's truck at a Pennsylvania repair site. The incidents involved different workers, different locations, and different safety records.
call: Is permissive joinder under Rule 20 proper merely because both plaintiffs sue the same roofing company?

choices.A: No, because Rule 20 requires all plaintiffs to be citizens of the same state.
choices.B: No, because the claims do not arise out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences.
choices.C: Yes, because plaintiffs with claims against the same defendant may always join in one action.
choices.D: Yes, because both claims use the same negligence theory.

rightExplanation: Rule 20 permits plaintiffs to join only if their claims arise out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences and share at least one common question of law or fact. Daniel's pallet accident and Martha's ladder accident happened months apart, at different sites, with different crews and records. The same corporate defendant and the same negligence label do not connect the operative facts into one transaction or series. Joinder is therefore improper.

wrongExplanations.A: Same-state citizenship sounds procedural, and federal joinder often overlaps with jurisdiction concepts. Rule 20 does not impose a same-citizenship requirement for plaintiffs.
wrongExplanations.C: Naming one defendant gives the claims a surface connection and makes one lawsuit seem efficient. Rule 20 still requires transactional relatedness, not just a shared defendant.
wrongExplanations.D: A shared negligence theory creates a common legal vocabulary. The rule also requires related operative facts, and these accidents have separate proof.
